chapter: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
title: A forgettable dance school job, then Benny Carter at the Arcadia
summary: After a dull job at another dancing school he joined Carter, whose four-part saxophone writing was instructive and ended the era of three-part saxes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Then you went to another dance school.

Yeah, yeah. I worked there awhile and -- well, this was before Benny Carter. Yeah, I worked in a -- it wasn't a -- it was just a job. It wasn't too big. Nothing historical happened on this job. It was just a thing to help me on my way, as a matter of speaking.

And after I got through with this job there, then I -- then I joined Benny Carter. Of course Benny Carter was working at the Arcadia Ballroom. And that was a very, very -- very instructive, you know. That helped me greatly because Benny was making these great arrangements at that time, and then this was a time when before that most bands had three-part

saxophones. They played three part harmony. And it was just about that time that four part harmony came in, and as I remember it's a funny thing -- and that was the end of a whole lot of piano players, because they couldn't read the four part harmony on the piano, you know. So then a whole brand new -- it was a whole turnaround because musicians who were better schooled than the ones who were predominant before that, you know, then they came to power. But Benny was one of the first to write four part harmony for saxophones. Yeah. And I used to you know, take a crack at all of them, first part, second part and whatever, you know, and I was learning how to transpose on the saxophone. You know, every aspect of the business I was trying very hard to learn. It was hard. It was hard in a way, but after I got into it it came easy, you know, and I used to do a lot of practicing in the daytime, you know, and that sort of thing. I'd practice what I'd come across or discovered the night before.
